hints.text: Use the power rule on each term: bring the exponent down in front and lower it by one. What happens to a constant?
Differentiating term by term gives $f'(x) = 12x^2 - 2$. Now substitute $x = 2$ into this derivative.
Substituting gives $12(4) - 2 = 46$, so the value of the derivative is $f'(2) = 46$.

explanation: Differentiate term by term with the power rule: $\frac{d}{dx}(4x^3) = 12x^2$, $\frac{d}{dx}(-2x) = -2$, $\frac{d}{dx}(7) = 0$.
Adding the pieces gives the derivative $f'(x) = 12x^2 - 2$.
Substitute $x = 2$ into the derivative to get the answer: $f'(2) = 12(4) - 2 = 46$.

alternativeExplanations.title: Why the $7$ disappears
steps: Adding $7$ slides the whole graph up without changing any slope.
The derivative measures slope, so a constant contributes $0$.
Only the $4x^3$ and $-2x$ terms carry slope: $12x^2 - 2$, which is $46$ at $x = 2$.
